As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience.

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI

Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything.

A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs. events.excerpt: # Release v5.23.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling2 Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) * Add inkling2 (#50682) by @guarin in [#50682](https://github.com/huggingface/transforme

These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. Abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. events.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.25000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.
  At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.

events.excerpt:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...]

Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

— Levent Alpöge, alpo.ge/remark.pdf

events.excerpt:
### Features

* **api:** add the image_dimensions_too_large error code


### Bug Fixes

* **bedrock:** send the user profile ID in the request body

  Amazon Bedrock reads `user_profile_id` from the request body and ignores the `anthropic-user-profile-id` header, so a profile ID given to `AnthropicBedrock` or `AsyncAnthropicBedrock` was not applied. Both clients now move it into the body of Messages requests and no longer send the header. A `user_profile_id` already in the body takes priority over the header.

  Some models on Bedrock do not support user profiles. A request to one of them with a profile ID now fails with a 400 error; before, the ID was ignored. Leave the ID off requests to those models.


### Chores

* **docs:** clarify billing_policy in batches and two billing errors

mtmd: drama3 voice cloning (#32586)

* mtmd: drama3 voice cloning

The Fish S2 codec encoder (fish_s2_spkenc) now also serves drama3:
- conversion: drama3 writes the codec encoder and the audio encoder KV, shared with fish_s2
- fish_s2_spkenc: outputs the codes of the clip (gen-side reference) and, in a drama3_gen mmproj,
  builds the drama3 backbone rows (E_lm[semantic] + E_cb[1][code 1]) / sqrt(2)
- drama3_gen tower: teacher forcing when the caller gives the codes of the next frame
- drama3 pipeline: reference-bracket-v1 prompt with one reference (vLLM-Omni fish_omni), the
  reference frames go through the backbone as codec rows and through the tower with their codes
- mtmd_gen_state_get_ref_codes(): read-only access to the reference codes of a gen state
